findings.commentary: Fixed on this line. Platform 25.3.5 pins @vaadin/rich-text-editor 25.3.5, whose vendored Quill escapes the video and formula values before building the semantic HTML, and the reproduction that fires on 25.3.4 does not fire here. The patched copy keeps Quill's own version string 2.0.3, because the fix is ours and there is no Quill release to move to, so a scanner reading the bundled file reports the advisory on this version anyway. CVE-2026-120350 names this same flaw: it is the advisory Vaadin itself published for it, and CVE-2025-15056 is the id under which it was first reported, so a scanner may lead with either. One record, one fix, and this verdict answers both ids.

findings.commentary: Fixed in Vaadin 25.3.1. Vaadin Charts pins Highcharts 12.2.0 exactly, and of the advisories Highsoft disclosed on 29 September 2026, all five reach Highcharts 12.2.0: writes to Object.prototype through dotted series.keys paths, and cross site scripting through credits.href, breadcrumbs.style, HTML text parsing while printing, and xlink:href in exported charts. Vaadin published this as CVE-2026-107588.
findings.impact: None on Vaadin 25.3.1 and later. On earlier 25.3 releases, chart options that carry data an attacker controls can run script in the viewer's browser or pollute Object.prototype, as each advisory describes.

findings.commentary: The parser is in the jar and nothing in a Vaadin application hands it an incoming header. From 25.3, opentelemetry-api 1.62.0 arrives through TestBench, whose Selenium client only adds trace context to the requests it sends, and Observability Kit no longer uses OpenTelemetry or an agent. The advisory needs incoming tracestate headers to reach W3CTraceContextPropagator.extract, which happens only if you add tracing of your own: Spring Boot OpenTelemetry tracing, the OpenTelemetry Java agent, or code that extracts trace context from requests.
findings.impact: None unless your application adds tracing that extracts W3C trace context from incoming requests. There anybody who can send a request can make each one cost CPU through a crafted tracestate header.

From 25.3, opentelemetry-api 1.62.0 arrives through TestBench, whose Selenium client only adds trace context to the requests it sends, and Observability Kit no longer uses OpenTelemetry or an agent. The advisory needs incoming tracestate headers to reach W3CTraceContextPropagator.extract, which happens only if you add tracing of your own: Spring Boot OpenTelemetry tracing, the OpenTelemetry Java agent, or code that extracts trace context from requests.
packages.impact: None unless your application adds tracing that extracts W3C trace context from incoming requests. There anybody who can send a request can make each one cost CPU through a crafted tracestate header.
packages.workaround: If you add such tracing, set <opentelemetry.version>1.67.0</opentelemetry.version> in your pom, which resolves the api and the SDK at 1.67.0 under the Spring Boot parent, or cap or remove the tracestate header at your proxy before requests reach the application.

findings.commentary: Your scanner has matched the wrong artifact. The advisory is unsafe deserialization of the incremental cache of KAPT, the annotation processing plugin of the Kotlin build tooling, and the advisory database names only org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-gradle-plugin. The CPE jetbrains:kotlin covers every artifact JetBrains publishes under that name, so the scanner reported it on kotlin-stdlib, which does not contain that code. The range is open because no version of kotlin-stdlib carries it. Nothing to upgrade for it.
